name: dietlibc (qsort and bsearch)
workload: qsort and bsearch of 1000 random ints, measured in CPU cycles, as recorded in the dietlibc 0.8 changelog entry.
claimed_speedup: qsort 300010 cycles vs glibc 679414 cycles (about 2.3x fewer cycles, derived from page data); bsearch 553 cycles vs glibc 3352 cycles (about 6.1x fewer cycles, derived from page data). Changelog author: 'I have no idea why glibc is so slow.'
stars_or_usage: 130 stars on the unofficial ensc git-cvs mirror (archived 2023-09-05); packaged by Debian, Fedora, Gentoo, openSUSE per search results
tradeoffs: A libc built for the smallest static Linux binaries (the dietlibc README says to use it for programs that do not need the bloat of glibc). Static linking only, GCC-only, no FreeBSD/Solaris/Windows support (FAQ), GPL-2.0-or-later licence, so statically linked programs carry the GPL. The qsort/bsearch comparison is a data point for the libc's small routines; the project's headline claim is size, not speed.
caveats: First-party, one changelog line from the 0.8 release (roughly 2001) with no compiler, flags, CPU model or glibc version stated. glibc's qsort and bsearch implementations have changed since then, so the ratio is probably obsolete. Size is dietlibc's real selling point and is not benchmarked in the repo (hello-world sizes appear only in search-result snippets of third-party slides, not opened). The FAQ also says dietlibc can 'improve performance by an order of magnitude for certain programming models' and points to fefe.de/fnord/SPEED and talk.pdf for benchmarks; those pages were not reachable here (EGRESS_BLOCKED). The same changelog notes an i386 strlen that is '31% faster, 14% smaller', but its baseline is the older dietlibc C version, not glibc. The official site fefe.de/dietlibc was EGRESS_BLOCKED here; repo_url is the unofficial ensc mirror whose last commit (2019-03-18) may lag upstream releases, so maintenance_status is left unknown.

name: Discount
workload: Convert an 11 MB Markdown file (Pro Git first edition sources concatenated across localizations) to HTML; wall time is the difference between running with the input and with no input, median of ten runs, in the cmark project's benchmark table.
claimed_speedup: discount 1.86 s vs Markdown.pl 2921.24 s (about 1570x faster, derived from page data); vs peg-markdown 5.45 s (about 2.9x faster, derived from page data); vs Python markdown 291.25 s (about 157x, derived from page data); vs PHP markdown 20.82 s (about 11x, derived from page data). In the same table cmark takes 0.36 s and sundown 0.34 s, both about 5x faster than discount.
hardware: 'ancient Thinkpad running Intel Core 2 Duo at 2GHz' (cmark benchmarks.md)
tradeoffs: Implements the original Markdown syntax (README: passes MarkdownTest_1.0, no CommonMark conformance claim) plus extensions; C library with command-line tools. Faster than scripting-language Markdown implementations but about 5x slower than cmark and sundown on the same input.
caveats: The numbers come from the cmark project's own benchmarks.md (tag 0.18), measured on an old Core 2 Duo laptop (cmark releases 0.13 to 0.18), not from Discount's repo, which has no benchmark. Discount version, compiler and flags are not stated; the benchmark driver is the public 'make bench' target in the cmark Makefile and the input is built from the public progit/progit repository. The cmark 0.13 table, opened too, gave discount 1.705 s on the same input; later cmark releases dropped Discount from the table. Markdown.pl is a regex-based Perl reference implementation, so beating it is a weak result; Discount is not the fastest C Markdown library (sundown and cmark are about 5x faster in the same cmark table).
